text: One hypothesis test at alpha equals 0.05 has a 5 percent chance of a false alarm when nothing is going on — a fair deal. But real analyses rarely stop at one test. An A/B test reports twenty metrics, a marketing analysis slices results by ten segments, a model search checks hundreds of features. Every extra test is another lottery ticket for a false alarm. This is the multiple comparisons problem.

If you run 20 independent tests where every null is true, the chance that at least one gives p under 0.05 is 1 minus 0.95 to the 20th power — about 64 percent. Simulating 1,000 experiments, each testing 20 metrics that truly don't differ, confirms it: about 62 percent of these nothing-is-happening experiments produced at least one significant metric, in line with the formula.

This is exactly how a team ends up celebrating a significant lift in a metric that was really just luck. There are two ways to define the goal. Family-wise error rate is the probability of at least one false discovery in the whole family of tests — strict, for when a single false claim is costly. False discovery rate is the expected proportion of your discoveries that are false — more lenient, better suited to exploratory work with many tests.

Now a realistic experiment: 20 metrics, where 6 truly move by 0.7 standard deviations and 14 do nothing. Uncorrected testing flags 8 metrics as significant — but 2 of those are false alarms, and in real life you wouldn't know which ones.

Bonferroni tests each hypothesis at alpha divided by the number of tests — simple, controls the family-wise rate, but conservative. Holm sorts p-values smallest to largest, comparing progressively looser thresholds and stopping at the first failure — it controls the same thing as Bonferroni but is never less powerful.

Benjamini-Hochberg sorts p-values and finds the largest rank whose p-value stays under a sliding threshold, declaring that one and everything smaller significant — it controls the false discovery rate, not the family-wise rate.

Applying all three to our 20 metrics: Bonferroni flags 5, zero false alarms. Holm flags 5, zero false alarms. Benjamini-Hochberg flags 6, zero false alarms. All three corrections removed both false alarms completely. Bonferroni and Holm found 5 of the 6 real effects; Benjamini-Hochberg found all 6.

That's the trade-off — stricter control means more missed effects, lower power. This is one illustrative run, not a general ranking, and libraries like statsmodels provide ready-made versions of all three corrections.

Prevention beats correction. Decide your primary metric before the experiment — one pre-declared metric needs no correction, the rest are exploratory. Pre-register the comparisons you plan to make, and count every test you run, including the ones you didn't end up reporting. Segment-slicing after the fact is especially dangerous, because the number of possible slices is enormous.

To recap: each test carries its own false-alarm risk, and the risks accumulate — 20 true nulls give about a 64 percent chance of at least one significant result. Bonferroni and Holm control the chance of any false discovery; Benjamini-Hochberg controls the proportion of false discoveries and keeps more power. The best defense is planning your comparisons in advance. Next chapter: from testing differences to asking whether one variable is related to another, and whether that relationship means cause.
